title: India's economy just grew faster than the central bank expected. November 4, 2026.
excerpt: From a woman who multiplied 13-digit numbers in her head, to an India-born mayor of a Canadian mountain town, to GDP growth that beat the RBI's own forecast, to a Padma Shri recipient who has walked into 550 villages over 40 years - November 4's four stories are about outperforming what anyone expected, including the experts.
bodyHtml:
Every story today is about beating an expectation someone else had already set - a calculator's speed, a town's assumptions about who runs for mayor, a central bank's own forecast, and four decades of nobody else showing up.

She multiplied two 13-digit numbers in 28 seconds. No calculator, no paper

Shakuntala Devi, the 'Human Computer,' was born November 4, 1929, in Bangalore. In June 1980, Imperial College London's Computer Department verified her multiplying two randomly generated 13-digit numbers correctly in 28 seconds - a feat that entered the 1982 Guinness Book of World Records.

He was born in India. In October 2026, he was elected mayor of a Canadian mountain town

Harshan Ramadass was elected Mayor of Fernie, British Columbia, on October 17, 2026, winning 54.5% of the vote after previously serving as a city councillor - one of at least two Indo-Canadian leaders elected mayor in BC's 2026 municipal elections.

India's economy just grew faster than the central bank expected

India's real GDP grew 7.8% in Q1 FY27 (April-June 2026), beating the RBI's own 7% forecast and up from 6.9% a year earlier. Investment rose 11.9% and exports rose 12%, both outpacing the headline number.

She has walked into roughly 550 villages in a Naxal-affected district most organizations avoided - for almost 40 years

Dr. Budhri Tati, known as 'Badi Didi,' has done grassroots tribal welfare work across Dantewada district, Chhattisgarh, since the mid-1980s - education, health and de-addiction work in villages most organizations avoided due to Naxal activity. She was named a Padma Shri recipient for 2026.

Four stories, one pattern: a mind faster than a calculator, a town that elected an India-born mayor, an economy that beat its own forecast, and a woman who kept walking into villages nobody else would visit.
